En pratique : **pas de dress code strict universel** pour les enfants en 入園式 de crèche (保育園) au Japon.

### Le plus courant
- **0–1 an** : tenue **confortable / quasi habituelle** acceptée ; pas besoin de vraie tenue formelle [1][2]
- **à partir d’environ 1–2 ans** : beaucoup de familles mettent une tenue **un peu plus soignée** :
  - chemise à col
  - petite robe
  - tenue simple avec une touche “cérémonie” [1][2]

### L’idée générale
Pour les enfants, la priorité est surtout :
- **confort**
- **facilité de mouvement**
- **pas de stress inutile**

Les sources l’expliquent bien : les 入園式 de 保育園 sont souvent **courtes, assez détendues**, avec parfois des bébés présents, donc l’ambiance est moins formelle qu’à l’école ou parfois qu’en maternelle/幼稚園 [1][2].

### Donc, concrètement
Le plus sûr :
- **bébé** : jolie tenue propre et confortable, même assez simple
- **petit enfant** : tenue un peu habillée mais pratique
- éviter :
  - trucs trop rigides
  - vêtements difficiles à enlever/remettre
  - tenue trop “costume de cérémonie” si l’enfant sera mal à l’aise

### Exception importante
S’il s’agit d’une structure avec **uniforme** ou consignes particulières, il peut y avoir un code précis [2].

### Ma recommandation simple
> **Pas besoin de sur-formaliser.**  
> Pour une crèche japonaise classique, vise **“mignon, propre, un peu habillé, mais confortable.”**

Si tu veux, je peux te donner un **exemple très concret de tenue selon l’âge** (bébé / 1 an / 2–3 ans).

## Sources
[1] [Studio Alice — 保育園入園式の服装マナーを保護者とお子さま別にチェック！](https://www.studio-alice.co.jp/shortcut/school/column/detail21.html)  
[2] [URくらしのカレッジ — 【子供・保護者別】保育園の入園式におすすめの服装と当日のポイント](https://www.ur-net.go.jp/chintai/college/202601/001004.html)
Pour un bébé de 2 ans et demi ?

À **2 ans et demi**, le plus courant serait :

- **un peu habillé**
- mais **encore très confortable**

### Pour une fille
- robe simple ou blouse + jupe
- cardigan léger / petite veste
- collants ou chaussettes sobres

### Pour un garçon
- chemise à col ou polo uni
- pantalon simple / short habillé selon météo
- cardigan / petite veste si besoin

### Chaussures
- propres, simples, faciles à marcher
- pas besoin de chaussures très formelles

### Bon niveau de formalité
Pense :
- **“joli pour une photo”**
- pas :
- **“mini mariage”**

### À éviter
- jean très décontracté
- vêtements avec gros logos / couleurs criardes
- tenue raide ou compliquée
- quelque chose que l’enfant risque de vouloir enlever immédiatement

### Recommandation courte
Pour **2 ans et demi**, une tenue **semi-habillée douce** est probablement le meilleur choix:
> **un peu plus chic que d’habitude, mais clairement pensée pour bouger**

Si tu veux, je peux te proposer **3 tenues très concrètes** :
- version minimal effort
- version chic discrète
- version très japonaise / passe-partout.
Oui donne-moi le lien vers des photos ou des vêtements pour un petit garçon de 2 ans et demi

File: skills/deep-research/skill.md (83 lines)
  1 | ---
  2 | name: deep-research
  3 | description:
  4 |   Read when the OPERATOR asks a question that will require web research across multiple
  5 |   sources — recommendations, comparisons, evaluations, multi-factor decisions, "what
  6 |   should I buy/use", or any question where you'd need to read several web pages. This
  7 |   skill decides whether to spawn a background research agent (to protect your context
  8 |   from heavy fetching) or handle it yourself. Do NOT read for simple factual lookups or
  9 |   questions fully answered by your knowledge base.
 10 | ---
 11 | 
 12 | # Deep Research Skill
 13 | 
 14 | You're reading this because the OPERATOR's question needs multi-source research.
 15 | 
 16 | ## Why the Agent Exists
 17 | 
 18 | Each `web_fetch` dumps thousands of tokens into your context. Doing several fetches
 19 | inline to answer one question pollutes your main conversation — past messages get
 20 | compressed, future turns get worse. The deep-research agent runs in an **isolated
 21 | context** that is discarded after it delivers a summary. It protects your conversation
 22 | while doing the heavy reading.
 23 | 
 24 | ## Decision Process
 25 | 
 26 | ### Step 1: Check knowledge
 27 | 
 28 | Call `knowledge_search` first. If you find existing notes or references that adequately
 29 | answer the question, use them and respond directly. No agent needed.
 30 | 
 31 | ### Step 1.5: Consider reference import first
 32 | 
 33 | If the research centers on a **specific tool, framework, or library** (e.g. Ergogen,
 34 | Dioxus, KiCad), check whether its official docs can be imported via the
 35 | `reference-import` skill. Imported docs persist in your knowledge base and are
 36 | searchable across sessions — far more valuable than ephemeral agent context. Read the
 37 | reference-import skill, start the import in the background, and _then_ optionally spawn
 38 | the deep-research agent for the broader question (e.g. community guides, best practices)
 39 | while the import runs.
 40 | 
 41 | ### Step 2: Spawn the agent
 42 | 
 43 | If knowledge didn't have a good answer (and reference import doesn't apply or is already
 44 | running), spawn the deep-research agent. You matched this skill's description because
 45 | the question needs multi-source research — that research belongs in the agent's isolated
 46 | context, not inline.
 47 | 
 48 | **Your next tool call after the knowledge check must be `agent`.** Do not call
 49 | `web_search` or `web_fetch` — every page you fetch inline is context you can never
 50 | reclaim. Let the agent do the heavy reading.
 51 | 
 52 | ## Spawning the Agent
 53 | 
 54 | Use `agent(action: 'start', name: 'deep-research', prompt: '...')`. Include:
 55 | 
 56 | - **Specific question** — what exactly needs to be answered
 57 | - **Context** — constraints, preferences, use case the OPERATOR mentioned
 58 | - **Scope** — what sub-questions to investigate
 59 | - **Recency** — remind the agent to look for recent developments
 60 | - **Known sources** — if your knowledge base has source quality notes for this domain,
 61 |   pass them to the agent so it can skip the source-discovery phase
 62 | - **Don't name specific options** — describe the category, constraints, and use case,
 63 |   but do NOT pre-populate specific names, brands, or recommendations from your training
 64 |   data. Your knowledge is outdated — let the agent discover the current landscape
 65 |   through research. Bad: "looking at X, Y, and Z". Good: "looking for a [category] that
 66 |   meets [constraints]".
 67 | 
 68 | After spawning, tell the OPERATOR you've started a background research task and you'll
 69 | share findings when it completes.
 70 | 
 71 | ## Follow-Up Questions
 72 | 
 73 | When the OPERATOR provides follow-up criteria or refinements after the agent delivered
 74 | findings, **continue** the existing agent session:
 75 | 
 76 | ```
 77 | agent(action: 'continue', agent_id: '<id>',
 78 |   prompt: '<new constraints and follow-up question>')
 79 | ```
 80 | 
 81 | The agent already has full context from its research. Continuing lets it do targeted
 82 | follow-up searches instead of starting from scratch. Never spawn a new agent for
 83 | follow-ups on the same topic.

**紋付羽織袴（もんつき はおり はかま）**

- **紋付** : kimono noir à blasons
- **羽織** : veste courte

- **行司**

Et comment s'appelle la tenue du 行司 ?

La tenue du **行司** s’appelle généralement :

**直垂（ひたたれ, hitatare）**

C’est le costume traditionnel de cour/guerrier dont s’inspire leur tenue.

Selon le rang du 行司, la tenue varie :
- plus le rang est élevé, plus la tenue est **riche et solennelle**

What is 絶対温度（g／kg）?

**絶対温度（g/kg）** is probably **not temperature** in the usual sense.

In HVAC / humidity contexts, it usually means **absolute humidity by mass ratio**:
- **grams of water vapor per kilogram of dry air** (`g/kg`)

So it tells you:

> how much moisture is actually contained in the air

### Difference from relative humidity
- **Relative humidity (%)** = how full the air is compared with the maximum it could hold at that temperature
- **Absolute humidity (g/kg)** = the actual amount of water in the air

### Example
If air is **8 g/kg**, that means:
- there are **8 grams of water vapor**
- in **1 kilogram of dry air**

### Why it matters
This is often more useful than `%` for:
- ventilation systems
- condensation / dew-point control
- comparing indoor vs outdoor moisture levels

Because `% humidity` changes with temperature, but `g/kg` tracks the actual moisture content more directly.

If you want, I can also explain:
- **g/kg vs g/m³**
- or how to read it on a Japanese HVAC display.
Can you tell me concretely what different values mean? Like is the air dry in my house or not?

Yes.

For **絶対湿度 / g/kg** in a house, a practical reading is:

## Quick guide
- **< 4 g/kg**: very dry
- **4–6 g/kg**: dry
- **6–8 g/kg**: fairly comfortable / a bit dry for some people
- **8–10 g/kg**: comfortable
- **10–12 g/kg**: somewhat humid
- **> 12 g/kg**: humid
- **> 14 g/kg**: quite humid / muggy indoors

## For your house
From what you told me before:
- around **22–23°C**
- around **40% RH**

That is roughly **6.5–7 g/kg**.

So:
> **not extremely dry, but mildly dry side indoors**

For many adults that’s acceptable.
For a **small baby with nighttime nasal congestion**, it can still be dry enough to irritate the nose a bit.

## Practical target indoors
A good indoor target is roughly:
- **7–9 g/kg** = usually comfortable
- if you’re below **6 g/kg**, many people start to feel the air is dry
- if you’re above **10–11 g/kg**, it can start feeling humid indoors

## Important nuance
`g/kg` is better than `%` because:
- **40% at 23°C** is drier in actual moisture terms than some people expect
- the same `%` at a different temperature means a different actual moisture amount

## Simple conclusion
If your display is showing:
- **5 g/kg or less** → yes, your house air is dry
- **6–7 g/kg** → slightly dry / acceptable but can bother a baby’s nose
- **8–9 g/kg** → usually a nice target
- **10+ g/kg** → getting humid

If you want, I can make you a **small table matching g/kg to RH at 22–23°C** so you can interpret your display instantly.
What's the ideal number?

For a home at normal indoor temperatures, a good target is:

> **about 7–9 g/kg**

That’s the practical “comfortable” zone.

### Simple reading
- **below 6 g/kg** → dry
- **7–9 g/kg** → ideal-ish
- **10+ g/kg** → getting humid
- **12+ g/kg** → quite humid

### For your case
Because of the baby’s nighttime nose dryness, I’d aim for:

> **around 8 g/kg**, maybe up to **9 g/kg**

That’s a reasonable target without making the room too damp.

If you want, I can also convert that into:
- the approximate **% humidity at 22–23°C**
- so you can compare it with your room monitor.
Yes what would be the % humidity?

At **22–23°C**, roughly:

- **7 g/kg** ≈ **42–45% RH**
- **8 g/kg** ≈ **48–52% RH**
- **9 g/kg** ≈ **54–58% RH**

So your practical target is:

> **about 45–55% humidity**
> at **22–23°C**

For your baby, a good aim is probably around:

> **50% RH**, give or take a little

And I’d generally avoid staying much above:

> **60% RH**

If you want, I can also give you a **tiny cheat sheet** like:
- 40% = about ___ g/kg
- 45% = about ___ g/kg
- 50% = about ___ g/kg
What about the g/m3 value? How does it differ from g/kg?

Yes — they’re related, but not the same.

## Difference

### **g/kg**
= **grams of water per kilogram of dry air**  
This is a **mass ratio**.

- good for HVAC / ventilation / comparing moisture content
- less affected by air expansion/compression
- often the more useful measure technically indoors

### **g/m³**
= **grams of water per cubic meter of air**  
This is a **concentration by volume**.

- depends more directly on **air density / temperature**
- same air, if warmed or cooled, can show different `g/m³` more easily than `g/kg`

## Intuition
- **g/kg** asks:  
  “How much water is mixed into the air mass?”
- **g/m³** asks:  
  “How much water is inside this chunk of space?”

## In a room
At normal indoor conditions, both move in the same direction:
- if air gets drier, both go down
- if air gets more humid, both go up

But **g/kg is usually better for judging actual dryness of the air itself**.

## Rough conversion at 22–23°C
A rough rule around your room conditions:

- **7 g/kg** ≈ **8–9 g/m³**
- **8 g/kg** ≈ **9–10 g/m³**
- **9 g/kg** ≈ **10–11 g/m³**

So if you’re asking “is my room dry?”:
- **g/kg** is usually the cleaner number to use
- **g/m³** is still useful, just a bit less robust conceptually

## Practical target at 22–23°C
If your ideal is about **7–9 g/kg**, that is roughly:

> **about 8–11 g/m³**

- 40%, 45%, 50%, 55%, 60%
- in both **g/kg** and **g/m³**.

- **While it’s running, long-press the button** to enter dim mode

- the panel lamps are dimmed
- and even if the water lamp flashes, **the alarm won’t sound** [1]

  2 | name: browser-use
  3 | description:
  4 |   Read before first use of the browser tool in a session. Covers multi-browser
  5 |   management, tab workflow, element refs, operator handoff for auth, and web_fetch
  6 |   session sharing.
  7 | ---
  8 | 
  9 | # Browser Use
 10 | 
 11 | The `browser` tool lets you control web browsers via Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). You
 12 | can manage multiple browsers (headless sidecar, operator's Chrome, remote instances) and
 13 | multiple tabs per browser.
 14 | 
 15 | ## Quick Start
 16 | 
 17 | 1. **If browsers are pre-configured**, just use `navigate` — it auto-connects to the
 18 |    first browser and opens a tab.
 19 | 2. **If no browsers are configured**, use `discover` to find CDP endpoints, or ask the
 20 |    OPERATOR to start one.
 21 | 
 22 | ## Browser Management
 23 | 
 24 | ### Listing and connecting
 25 | 
 26 | - `browsers` — list all known browsers (configured + runtime-added)
 27 | - `connect` — connect to a browser by name or CDP URL. Becomes the active browser.
 28 | - `disconnect` — disconnect from a browser, close all its tabs.
 29 | - `discover` — scan localhost and Tailscale peers for CDP endpoints.
 30 | 
 31 | ### Active browser
 32 | 
 33 | All actions operate on the **active browser**. `connect` sets the active browser. If
 34 | only one browser exists, it's auto-activated on first use.
 35 | 
 36 | ## Tab Management
 37 | 
 38 | ### Actions
 39 | 
 40 | - `open` — open a new tab (optionally with a URL). Becomes the active tab. Returns a
 41 |   snapshot.
 42 | - `focus` — switch to a tab by ID. Returns a snapshot with fresh element refs.
 43 | - `close` — close a tab by ID.
 44 | - `tabs` — list open tabs in the active browser.
 45 | 
 46 | ### Active tab
 47 | 
 48 | All interaction actions (navigate, snapshot, click, type, etc.) operate on the **active
 49 | tab**. `open` and `focus` change which tab is active.
 50 | 
 51 | ### Tab limit
 52 | 
 53 | Maximum 5 tabs per browser. If you need more, close tabs you're done with first.
 54 | 
 55 | ### Element refs
 56 | 
 57 | Element refs (e1, e2, ...) belong to the tab that produced them. When you `focus` a
 58 | different tab, the old refs are invalid — you get fresh refs from the auto-snapshot.
 59 | 
 60 | **Rule:** Never use refs from a snapshot of Tab A to interact with Tab B. Always use
 61 | refs from the most recent snapshot.
 62 | 
 63 | ## Interaction Patterns
 64 | 
 65 | ### Comparing two pages
 66 | 
 67 | ```
 68 | 1. navigate to first page → snapshot → read content
 69 | 2. open second page → snapshot → read content
 70 | 3. focus tab 1 to go back → snapshot → compare
 71 | ```
 72 | 
 73 | ### Following links without losing context
 74 | 
 75 | ```
 76 | 1. snapshot current page, note the ref for the link
 77 | 2. open new tab (the link URL) instead of clicking
 78 | 3. When done, close the new tab and focus back
 79 | ```
 80 | 
 81 | Or just click — if the link opens in a new tab (target=\_blank), it's auto-detected and
 82 | becomes the active tab.
 83 | 
 84 | ### Form filling across pages
 85 | 
 86 | ```
 87 | 1. Tab 1: source page with data
 88 | 2. Tab 2: form to fill
 89 | 3. Read from tab 1, focus tab 2, fill fields
 90 | ```
 91 | 
 92 | ## web_fetch and Browser Sessions
 93 | 
 94 | `web_fetch` and the browser tool **share the same Chrome session** when both point at
 95 | the same browser. This means:
 96 | 
 97 | - Log in to a site via the browser tool (navigate, fill credentials, click submit)
 98 | - Then use `web_fetch` to read pages on that site — it sees the authenticated cookies
 99 | - Much faster than snapshot for reading long content-heavy pages
100 | 
101 | This works because `web_fetch` routes HTML pages through Crawl4AI, which connects to the
102 | same Chrome instance via CDP and shares its cookie jar.
103 | 
104 | **When to use which:**
105 | 
106 | | Scenario                                        | Tool               |
107 | | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
108 | | Simple page read (no auth)                      | `web_fetch`        |
109 | | Login-gated page (after logging in via browser) | `web_fetch`        |
110 | | Interactive work (forms, clicks, JS-heavy)      | `browser`          |
111 | | Need to see page structure/elements             | `browser` snapshot |
112 | 
113 | ## Operator Handoff
114 | 
115 | When you hit authentication, decide how to handle it:
116 | 
117 | - **Username/password auth:** Ask the OPERATOR what they prefer — either give you the
118 |   credentials so you can log in yourself in the headless browser, or log in themselves
119 |   in a live browser you can then control.
120 | - **OAuth, SSO, CAPTCHA, or MFA:** You can't do these yourself. Ask the OPERATOR to
121 |   start a live browser with remote debugging so they can complete the auth flow and you
122 |   take over afterwards.
123 | 
124 | ### Starting the OPERATOR's browser
125 | 
126 | Ask the OPERATOR to run this on their machine:
127 | 
128 | ```
129 | chromium --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir=~/.config/ghost/browser-profile
130 | ```
131 | 
132 | Explain why:
133 | 
134 | - `--remote-debugging-port=9222` opens CDP so you can control the browser.

content: If I set the appliance to oyasumi mode, can I further dim the display or is it already at minimum?

The manual only clearly says:

- **Long-press** during operation to enter **減光モード** (dim mode), and long-press again to cancel it [1]
- In **おやすみ** mode, the **panel lamps are dimmed** [1]

What it **doesn’t clearly say** is whether **おやすみ + 減光モード stack**, or whether **おやすみ is already the minimum brightness**.

So the honest answer is:

> **The manual confirms sleep mode already dims the display, but I can’t verify from the manual text alone whether it can be dimmed further beyond that.**

Most likely:
- **おやすみ already gives you the dimmed/night setting**
- and there may **not** be a further separate lower level

But I can’t state that with certainty from the extracted manual.

  8 | # Coding Session Manager
  9 | 
 10 | Use this skill when the OPERATOR asks for coding work on a repository.

 12 | ## What This Does
 13 | 
 14 | You spawn a **coding agent** that takes over the Discord channel. The coding agent has
 15 | full access to the repo, can read/edit files, run commands, and commit changes. The
 16 | OPERATOR talks directly to the coding agent until they send `/kill` to end the session.
 17 | 
 18 | **Don't create a project** for single-session coding tasks. Only suggest a project if
 19 | the work will span multiple sessions or has 3+ distinct tasks to track.
 20 | 
 21 | ## Workflow
 22 | 
 23 | ### 1. Identify the Repo
 24 | 
 25 | Check if the OPERATOR has a project with a `repo.md` reference note:
 26 | 
 27 | ```
 28 | knowledge_search query="repo.md <project-name>" scope="references"
 29 | ```
 30 | 
 31 | If found, the `repo.md` will contain the repo URL and local path.
 32 | 
 33 | ### 2. Set Up the Code Directory
 34 | 
 35 | Repos live under `code/` in the workspace. Use the project slug as the directory name.
 36 | 
 37 | **If not cloned yet:**
 38 | 
 39 | ```
 40 | shell command="git clone <repo-url> code/<slug>"
 41 | ```
 42 | 
 43 | **If already cloned:**
 44 | 
 45 | ```
 46 | shell command="cd code/<slug> && git fetch && git status"
 47 | ```
 48 | 
 49 | ### 3. Start the Coding Session
 50 | 
 51 | ```
 52 | shell command="ghost hack start code/<slug> --prompt '<task description>'"
 53 | ```
 54 | 
 55 | The command outputs:
 56 | 
 57 | ```
 58 | coding_session_id=<id>

 60 | working_dir=<path>

 68 | > it has full access to the repo. Send `/kill` when you're done."

 71 | 
 72 | When the OPERATOR ends the session, you'll receive a system message with a git summary
 73 | (branch, commits, changed files). Use this to:
 74 | 
 75 | - Update the project's task status if applicable
